items.title: IS Auditing: Purpose, Charter and the Audit Universe
items.summary: This lesson introduces information systems auditing: what it is, why organisations need it, how an audit charter works, and how to build an audit universe.
objectives: Define information systems auditing and distinguish it from other assurance activities
Explain the purpose and contents of an IS audit charter
Build an audit universe for a fictional organisation
Explain risk-based audit planning

sections.heading: What IS auditing is
sections.body: Information systems auditing is the independent examination of an organisation's information systems, processes and controls. It answers: are systems working as intended, are risks managed, and is the organisation compliant?
bullets: Independent: the auditor is not responsible for the area audited

sections.heading: IS audit vs other assurance
sections.body: IS auditing differs from internal audit, external audit and security assessment.
bullets: Internal audit: broader scope, reports to the board
External audit: financial statements, reports to shareholders
IS audit: focuses on IT systems and controls
Security assessment: technical testing, not assurance

sections.heading: The IS audit charter
sections.body: The charter is the document that authorises the audit function.
bullets: Purpose: why the audit function exists
Scope: what systems and processes are covered
Authority: what the auditor can access
Reporting line: to whom the auditor reports
Independence: safeguards against conflicts of interest

sections.heading: Building the audit universe
sections.body: The audit universe is the complete list of systems, processes and locations that could be audited.

sections.heading: Risk-based audit planning
sections.body: Not everything can be audited every year. Prioritise by risk.
bullets: Low-risk systems: audit every 3 years or on change

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Write a short IS audit charter for a fictional company. Identify 5 audit areas for the audit universe.

practicalExercise.title: IS audit charter and audit universe
practicalExercise.brief: Write a short IS audit charter for a fictional company and list 5 audit areas.
steps: Draft charter sections (purpose, scope, authority, reporting)
List 5 audit areas with risk ratings
practicalExercise.deliverable: A charter document and audit universe table.

references: ISACA CISA Domain 1: Information Systems Auditing Process

items.title: Audit Planning: Objectives, Scope and Sampling
items.summary: This lesson covers how to plan an IS audit: setting objectives, defining scope, selecting sampling methodology, and creating an audit plan.
objectives: Explain how to set audit objectives
Define audit scope and boundaries
Describe sampling methodology for IS audits
Create an audit plan for a fictional engagement

sections.heading: Setting audit objectives
sections.body: Audit objectives define what the audit will achieve.

sections.heading: Defining audit scope
sections.body: Scope determines what is in and out of the audit.
bullets: Time period: which quarter or year?

sections.heading: Sampling methodology
sections.body: Auditors cannot test everything. Sampling selects a representative subset.
bullets: Judgmental sampling: auditor selects based on expertise
Attribute sampling: tests for presence or absence
Variable sampling: tests for amounts or values
table: What is the average transaction value?

sections.heading: Creating the audit plan
sections.body: The audit plan documents how the audit will be conducted.
bullets: Resources: who will perform the audit?

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Write an audit plan for a payroll system audit. Include objectives, scope, sampling approach and timeline.

practicalExercise.title: Payroll system audit plan
practicalExercise.brief: Write an audit plan for a payroll system audit.

references: IIA International Standards for the Professional Practice of Internal Auditing

items.title: IT General Controls: Access, Change and Operations
items.summary: IT General Controls (ITGC) are the foundation of IT audit. This lesson covers logical access controls, change management, backup and recovery, and operations controls.
objectives: Explain what ITGC are and why they matter
Describe logical access control testing
Describe change management control testing
Describe backup and recovery control testing

sections.heading: What ITGC are
sections.body: ITGC are controls that apply to all systems, not just one application. They support application controls.
bullets: Logical access: who can access systems?
Change management: how are changes approved?
Operations: how are systems run daily?
Backup and recovery: can data be restored?

sections.heading: Logical access controls
sections.body: Access controls ensure only authorised people can access systems.
bullets: User provisioning: access granted on approval
Access reviews: periodic review of access

sections.heading: Change management controls
sections.body: Change management ensures changes are authorised and tested.
bullets: Change approval: authorised by appropriate person

sections.heading: Backup and recovery controls
sections.body: Backup and recovery ensure data can be restored after loss.

sections.heading: Operations controls
sections.body: Operations controls ensure systems run correctly day to day.
bullets: Job scheduling: batch jobs run on time
Incident management: issues logged and resolved

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Write a short ITGC audit programme for a fictional company. Identify 5 controls to test and the evidence to review.
bullets: Control 1: User access reviews - evidence: review minutes
Control 2: Change approval - evidence: change tickets
Control 3: Backup verification - evidence: restore logs

practicalExercise.title: ITGC audit programme
practicalExercise.brief: Write an ITGC audit programme for a fictional company.

items.title: Application Controls: Input, Processing and Output
items.summary: Application controls are specific to individual applications. This lesson covers input, processing, output and interface controls, and how to test them.
objectives: Explain the difference between ITGC and application controls
Describe input, processing and output controls
Describe interface controls
Explain how to test application controls

sections.heading: ITGC vs application controls
sections.body: ITGC apply to all systems. Application controls apply to specific applications.
bullets: Both are needed for reliable systems

sections.heading: Input controls
sections.body: Input controls ensure data entered into the system is valid and complete.
bullets: Validation: check data format and range

sections.heading: Processing controls
sections.body: Processing controls ensure data is processed correctly.
bullets: Batch controls: count and sum transactions

sections.heading: Output controls
sections.body: Output controls ensure results are accurate and distributed correctly.
bullets: Retention: keep output for required period

sections.heading: Interface controls
sections.body: Interface controls ensure data transferred between systems is accurate and complete.

sections.heading: Testing application controls
sections.body: Application controls are tested by walking through transactions.
bullets: Parallel testing: run old and new systems together
User interviews: ask users about their experience

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Design application controls for a fictional online banking transfer function.
bullets: Input: validate account numbers and amounts
Interface: reconcile with core banking system

practicalExercise.title: Application controls for online banking
practicalExercise.brief: Design application controls for an online banking transfer.

items.title: Audit Evidence: Collection, Testing and Workpapers
items.summary: This lesson covers evidence collection, testing procedures, sampling, and audit workpapers — the core of how an IS auditor proves findings.
objectives: Explain what audit evidence is and what makes it reliable
Describe evidence collection techniques
Explain how to test controls using evidence
Document findings in audit workpapers

sections.heading: What audit evidence is
sections.body: Audit evidence is the information the auditor uses to support findings and conclusions. It must be sufficient, reliable, relevant and useful.
bullets: Sufficient: enough evidence to support the conclusion
Relevant: relates to the audit objective
Useful: helps management understand the issue

sections.heading: Types of evidence
sections.body: Different types of evidence have different reliability.

sections.heading: Evidence collection techniques
sections.body: Auditors collect evidence through inspection, observation, inquiry and re-performance.

sections.heading: Testing controls
sections.body: Controls are tested by selecting a sample and checking each item for compliance.
bullets: Test each item: check for compliance
Record results: document what passed and failed
Evaluate: determine if the control operates effectively

sections.heading: Audit workpapers
sections.body: Workpapers are the auditor's record of what was done, what was found, and what it means.

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Write an evidence collection plan for a payroll system audit. Identify 3 evidence types, how to collect each, and what you expect to find.
bullets: Evidence 1: Payroll change tickets - review for approval
Evidence 3: User access list - verify authorized users

practicalExercise.title: Evidence collection plan
practicalExercise.brief: Write an evidence collection plan for a payroll system audit.

items.title: IT Operations: System Management and Problem Management
items.summary: This lesson covers IT operations controls: job scheduling, system monitoring, problem management, capacity management and system performance.
objectives: Explain IT operations controls and their audit focus
Describe job scheduling and system monitoring
Describe problem and incident management
Explain capacity management and performance monitoring

sections.heading: IT operations controls
sections.body: IT operations controls ensure systems run reliably day to day. Auditors test these to confirm systems are stable, available and well-managed.
bullets: Job scheduling: automated jobs run as planned
System monitoring: alerts detected and acted on
Problem management: root causes identified and fixed

sections.heading: Job scheduling
sections.body: Scheduled jobs (batch processing, backups, reports) must run on time and complete successfully.
bullets: Schedule documented: when each job runs
Exceptions handled: failures are logged and resolved
Changes controlled: schedule changes are approved

sections.heading: System monitoring
sections.body: Monitoring detects issues before they become incidents.
bullets: Alerts configured: thresholds set for key metrics
Alerts reviewed: someone watches the alerts
Escalation: issues are escalated when needed
Logs retained: monitoring data is kept for review

sections.heading: Problem and incident management
sections.body: Incidents are unplanned disruptions. Problems are root causes behind repeated incidents.

sections.heading: Capacity management
sections.body: Capacity management ensures IT resources meet current and future demand.
bullets: Demand forecast: what will be needed?
Planning: procure resources before they are needed

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Write an IT operations audit checklist for a fictional data centre. Include job scheduling, monitoring, problem management and capacity management.
bullets: Check: critical alerts are reviewed daily
Check: incidents have root cause analysis

practicalExercise.title: IT operations audit checklist
practicalExercise.brief: Write an IT operations audit checklist for a data centre.

items.title: Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Auditing
items.summary: This lesson covers BCP/DR auditing: BIA, RTO/RPO, recovery strategies, testing and the difference between business continuity and disaster recovery.
objectives: Explain the difference between business continuity and disaster recovery
Describe BIA, RTO, RPO and MTPD
Explain recovery strategies (hot/warm/cold sites)
Describe BCP/DR testing approaches

sections.heading: BCP vs DRP
sections.body: Business Continuity Planning (BCP) keeps the business running during a disruption. Disaster Recovery Planning (DRP) restores IT systems after a disaster.
bullets: DRP: IT-focused, restores systems and data
BCP includes DRP as a component

sections.heading: BIA fundamentals
sections.body: Business Impact Analysis identifies critical functions and the impact of losing them over time.
bullets: Critical functions: what must keep running?
Impact timeline: what happens after 4 hours, 24 hours, 1 week?

sections.heading: RTO, RPO, MTPD
sections.body: Key continuity metrics.
bullets: RTO: Recovery Time Objective - maximum acceptable downtime
RPO: Recovery Point Objective - maximum acceptable data loss
MTPD: Maximum Tolerable Period of Disruption - absolute limit

sections.heading: Recovery strategies
sections.body: Strategies for restoring operations after disruption.
bullets: Hot site: fully operational, ready immediately
Warm site: partially equipped, needs setup
Cold site: empty space, needs full build-out

sections.heading: BCP/DR testing
sections.body: Plans must be tested to prove they work.
bullets: Full interruption: actual system shutdown test

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Design a BCP/DR test plan for a fictional company. Include scope, scenarios, participants and success criteria.
bullets: Test 3: Full interruption - power outage simulation

practicalExercise.title: BCP/DR test plan
practicalExercise.brief: Design a BCP/DR test plan for a fictional company.

items.title: Logical Access Controls and Cryptographic Governance
items.summary: This lesson covers logical access controls: identification, authentication, authorisation, and cryptographic governance — how encryption keys are managed and audited.
objectives: Explain logical access controls: identification, authentication, authorisation
Describe authentication factors and multi-factor authentication
Explain cryptographic governance: key management, encryption standards
Describe how to audit access and cryptography controls

sections.heading: Logical access controls
sections.body: Logical access controls govern who can access systems and data, and what they can do.
bullets: Authorisation: what are you allowed to do?

sections.heading: Authentication factors
sections.body: Something you know, something you have, something you are.
bullets: Something you have: token, smart card, phone
Something you are: fingerprint, face, iris
MFA: combine two or more factors

sections.heading: Access provisioning and review
sections.body: Access must be granted on approval and reviewed periodically.
bullets: Provisioning: access granted based on role
Deprovisioning: access removed when no longer needed
Privileged access: admin accounts tightly controlled

sections.heading: Cryptographic governance
sections.body: Cryptography protects data confidentiality and integrity. Governance ensures keys are managed properly.
bullets: Key management: generation, storage, rotation, destruction
Key custodian: who is responsible for keys?
Key rotation: keys changed on schedule
table: Verify keys stored in HSM or vault
Verify keys destroyed when no longer needed

sections.heading: Auditing access controls
sections.body: Auditors test access controls by sampling user accounts and reviewing access logs.
bullets: Sample user accounts: verify access is appropriate
Review access logs: look for suspicious activity
Test terminated users: access removed promptly

sections.heading: Practical exercise
sections.body: Design an access control policy for a fictional company. Include identification, authentication, authorisation and accountability.
bullets: Identification: user ID required for all systems

practicalExercise.title: Access control policy
practicalExercise.brief: Design an access control policy for a fictional company.
